props.title: Let It Be

sections.content: Let It Be (1970) captures the Beatles' final days with raw, often uncomfortable intimacy. Director Michael Lindsay-Hogg's fly-on-the-wall approach documents the band recording their last album, revealing the creative tensions and personality conflicts that would lead to their breakup. The film's most iconic moment - the impromptu rooftop concert at Apple Records - became the Beatles' final public performance. This unplanned 42-minute set influenced later music documentaries like The Last Waltz (1978) and inspired the rooftop concert in Get Back (2021), Peter Jackson's expanded revisiting of the Let It Be footage.

sections.content: The film's troubled production mirrored the band's fracturing relationships. Originally conceived as a TV special called "Get Back" to document the Beatles returning to their roots, it morphed into a feature revealing their dissolution. Unlike polished music docs like A Hard Day's Night (1964), Let It Be's cinema verite style exposed uncomfortable moments - particularly tensions between Paul McCartney and George Harrison. This rawness influenced later warts-and-all band documentaries like Some Kind of Monster (2004) about Metallica's near-breakdown.

Let It Be's restoration and re-evaluation through Peter Jackson's Get Back (2021) offers fascinating contrasts in documentary approach. While Lindsay-Hogg's theatrical cut emphasized conflict and melancholy, Jackson's expanded version reveals more joy and creativity amid the tension. Together, they demonstrate how editing choices and historical context shape documentary narrative, similar to how What Happened, Miss Simone? (2015) and Amazing Grace (2018) use archival footage to tell different stories about their subjects. SUBHEAD: Impact on Music Documentary Style

sections.content: Let It Be pioneered an observational approach that influenced decades of music documentaries. Its unflinching look at creative conflict echoes through films like Dig! (2004), chronicling the rivalry between The Dandy Warhols and The Brian Jonestown Massacre, and End of the Century (2003) about The Ramones. The film's focus on the recording process, showing songs evolving from rough ideas to finished versions, set a template followed by everything from In the Studio (1985) about Stevie Ray Vaughan to Classic Albums series documentaries.
